In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of glutathione S-transferses (GSTs) in the metabolism of dichloromethylene to formaldehyde and the reaction of formaldehyde to DNA and RNA.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DCM is a rodent carcinogen and that the mechanism involves metabolism of DCM to HCHO and the subsequent reaction of HCHO with DNA and RNA in hepatocytes.

the GST-mediated metabolism of DCM to HCHO is required for its genotoxic effects in mice and that the formation of DPX and RFA in hepatocyte cultures is a useful model for the prediction of the genotoxicity of DCM in vivo.
DCM is a weak hepatocarcinogen in rodents and a weak hepatoclastogenic agent in humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the GST pathway for the metabolism of DCM to HCHO is important in mice but not in rats, hamsters, or humans, and that HCHO reacts primarily with RNA in all species.
DCM does not appear to pose a risk to humans, but the possibility that it might do so cannot be completely excluded.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the mouse liver is an inappropriate model for predicting human liver cancer risk from DCM exposure, because the mouse liver is more sensitive than the human liver to DCM.
